description_full: Hecla Mining Company, together with its subsidiaries, provides precious and base metals in the United States, Canada, Japan, Korea, China, and internationally. The company mines for silver, gold, lead, and zinc concentrates, as well as carbon material containing silver and gold for custom smelters, metal traders, and third-party processors; and unrefined doré containing silver and gold. The company was incorporated in 1891 and is headquartered in Coeur d'Alene, Idaho.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 1K people. Revenue per employee of $763K ranks in the above the sector median among Basic Materials peers, improving at 12%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $166K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $6K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 3× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (1/10).
financial_summary: Hecla Mining Company is a mid-cap basic materials business with a $9.9B market cap on $1.4B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +26% over the past three years and +12% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +3.7pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.

Returns on capital run at 3% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 17% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $310M in free cash flow — roughly 22 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.75× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 12× is fortress-like.

Net dilution runs at 2.1% annually, transferring value from owners to stock-based comp, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 36% operating margin runs 27pp above the Basic Materials median (10%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.76x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+43.9% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.04 across 219 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 26% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 9% over the last three months.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 57% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 72% and a beta of 1.11, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 2.24 vs 5y 1.25), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $582.9M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 53% in the 2020 crash, 52% in the 2022 bear market and 92% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $11.36 (margin of safety -30%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 76%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $6.07 to $21.47 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Basic Materials peers: P/FCF 31.9 vs 22.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 54% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.1% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 10 covering analysts target $21.68 on average, 47% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 3% falls short of the cost of capital of 10.3%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 2.24).
It runs a 17% gross margin and converts 22% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.75x.
ROE of 12% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.4x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 29pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 0.8% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $281.5M.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 7.1, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 25.6% over 3 years, 15.5% over 5 years and 12.4% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 21%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 3.0% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 28.1% a year over five years.
Capex runs 1.5x depreciation (17.7% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 37, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.6%), and institutions hold 77%.
Net share issuance leaves shareholder yield negative (-2.1%), diluting holders.
The share count has grown 7.1% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 15 consecutive years, raising it 3.8% a year over the last five.
people: With about 1,865 employees, each generates about $763K of revenue, 1.2x the Basic Materials median, and productivity has risen 11.6% a year.
That works out to $166K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.7M (3x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
